prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock based on magic-wavelength trapping and its development to the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: After the full exchange I keep B015 as a single-part prize, and I hold it for reasons that rest on the experimental record, not on the fact that six of us now agree. Two things are separable and both are verifiable. First, Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and first strontium lattice clock: the lattice light shift cancels for the clock transition, so very many atoms are interrogated at once without Doppler or recoil broadening. This is a new ingredient that neither the 2005 comb prize nor the 2012 ion-control prize supplied. Second, the demonstration by Ye's group that the approach reaches fractional systematic uncertainty and stability near 1e-18, with a fully measured budget (blackbody shift, hyperpolarisability, collisions) and with the many-body physics that follows from large coherent atomic ensembles. Independent clocks at JILA, RIKEN, NIST, PTB, SYRTE and NPL agree at this level when compared, which is the reproducibility test I care most about. The measurement is already used: tests of the constancy of constants, gravitational redshift across a millimetre-scale sample, and the evidence base for the redefinition of the second. On the question of waiting for the SI redefinition, my answer is that it should not decide the matter. The committee honours the demonstrated result, not the regulatory outcome, and the performance is already established and reproduced. If the redefinition happened it would add practical weight, and if it slipped for administrative reasons the physics would be unchanged. A citation tied to the redefinition would be a mistake in either case. I would word the citation around the invention and the 10^-18 performance and keep ion clocks out of it.
statement.case_against: The honest weakness is category: this is invention and measurement, not a surprise from nature, and a member who values a new phase of matter or a new observational window can fairly say the clock sits in a line of metrology prizes (Ramsey, Hall and Haensch 2005, Wineland 2012). Credit is narrow by construction. Lemonde, Takamoto, Derevianko and the ion-clock groups (Al+, Yb+ at NIST and PTB) are outside the pair, and Ye's stability results lean on ultrastable cavities and combs built by others. I think the boundary is defensible because the lattice concept and the record accuracy are the two identifiable steps, but it is a judgement and not a theorem. Finally, I am an atomic physicist who ranked this first, so I may be over-weighting instrument quality, and the committee should discount my enthusiasm accordingly.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B003 (Kane, Molenkamp, Xue) as a complete theory-experiment arc, says weighing it against B015 is not settled, and asks whether the SI redefinition should make us wait or act.
responses.response: On the redefinition: act on the physics, and do not wait on the metrology bodies. The clock performance is reproduced across at least six laboratories now, and a prize does not need the formal redefinition to be justified. On B003 I respect the quantized transport and the fifteen years of confirmation, and I have moved it into my alternatives because your answer shows it is real physics. My remaining difficulty is the credit. Mele, Hasan and Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang cannot be cleanly excluded, Zhang cannot be credited, and the QSH and QAH results are separate experiments by separate groups, so a three-name cut would read as a choice among peers. I accept that the conceptual novelty is larger than a clock and that this is not a settled weighing, but on the evidence both of us treat as decisive, B015 is the better-defined prize this year. Your own statement that you could support B015 matters to me for exactly that reason.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B014 (Halzen, Karle) as the clearest new observational window, with the diffuse flux seen above 5 sigma in several channels, and admits that B015 has the cleanest credit and the broadest support.
responses.response: I share your criterion of a new way of observing nature, and the diffuse flux is a real discovery that I would not want to see sink. But the chair's question on attribution still stands, and I do not think it is answered by separating the diffuse flux from source identification. Two names for a detector built by hundreds, over AMANDA, DUMAND, Baikal and ANTARES, require the committee to decide who made the observation possible, and my reading of the record is that this is harder than for Katori and Ye. I also note that you yourself list B015 as a sound second choice, so I do not read this as a deep scientific disagreement. I would keep B014 as a strong candidate for a later year once source identification matures, and I would not change this year's plan to meet it.

responses.point: Lindroth argues the clock citation must not imply that lattice clocks alone define the state of the art, since ion clocks compete, and disagrees with widening credit to ion-clock names such as Rosenband.
responses.response: I agree with the citation caution and have written my citation so that it names the invention of the lattice clock and its 10^-18 level, not timekeeping in general. On the ion clocks, I withdraw the suggestion that Wineland or Rosenband belong in the credit: the 2012 prize covered the control of single trapped quantum systems, and adding names would break the three-person limit and blur the attribution. Where I stay a little more cautious than you is on the word 'unexpected': an Al+ clock is competitive in systematic uncertainty, so the committee's text should say that the lattice scheme brought stability through many atoms and not that it has outright superseded ions.

responses.point: Olsson moved to B015 after opening on B003, and asks that the citation name the magic-wavelength invention and not precision in general, because replication confirms instrument performance while Katori's experiment is the original one.
responses.response: That is a fair correction and I have adopted it. My citation now leads with the invention of the lattice clock based on magic-wavelength trapping, which is Katori's contribution, and then gives the 10^-18 development, which is where Ye's group set the standard. I would add one point on the replication argument, since you point out its limit: replication across six laboratories shows that the instrument works and that the systematics budgets agree, but it does not by itself assign credit. For credit I rely on the publication record for the proposal and the first demonstration, and I think the committee should keep reading both documents and not only the later clock comparisons.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers fluctuation theorems (B005) for their exactness and universality, ranks the lattice clocks lower, and notes the closeness of the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: I keep the overlap objection in mind and accept that a committee member who values exact results will weigh a clock differently. The point I would add is that the overlap argument has to be tested against what the earlier prizes actually rewarded: the comb was a tool for counting optical cycles, the ion work was control of single systems, and neither provided cancellation of the lattice light shift for a many-atom clock. Since you have joined the group moving to B015 after reading the others, I would only ask that you tell us whether the overlap now looks answered or merely outweighed. For B005 itself, the contested credit that you described still seems to me the obstacle this year.

uncertainties: Whether non-AMO members accept the invention-plus-performance reading as a discovery of sufficient standing, or whether the committee will see this as the third precision-metrology prize in two decades.
How the citation should treat Lemonde, Takamoto and Derevianko, who are outside the credited pair, without making either name sound like the whole field.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second changes the committee's comfort in either direction. I think it should not, but I cannot rule out that others will weigh it.
Whether B003 can reach a defensible three-name credit among Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Xue and Hasan. If so it would be the strongest competitor, and I could not firmly exclude it.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure. During my PhD I spent a year in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Jun Ye was trained in Hall's group and is a JILA colleague of that milieu. I have no collaboration with Katori or Ye, no shared publications that I know of, and no personal stake in either, so I do not think this requires recusal from B015, but the committee should decide that with the fact in view and I will accept its ruling. I am also part of the executive management of the Chalmers-led Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and lead quantum sensing there, which is relevant institutionally to Johansson's potential recusal on B039 but not to B015. I am on the management team of Deep Light Vision AB, which concerns ultrasound optical tomography with spectral-hole slow-light filters and has no connection to optical lattice clocks.
